videos.title: Welcome: choose a small moment
videos.outline: An introduction to choice, privacy, free core features and the limits of MindPal.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
Welcome to MindPal. This is an AI-generated presenter. MindPal offers short wellbeing practices and optional reflection activities. You can choose a small step, or simply explore.

Some days you may want a few minutes. On other days, thirty seconds may be enough. You can skip the check-in, stop an exercise, or return another day. There is no streak to protect.

Writing is optional. Before saving personal information, check the privacy information for this version. Other people using the same device or browser may be able to see saved entries. You can reflect without typing anything into MindPal.

Any automated guide in MindPal is software, not a person or a therapist. MindPal cannot diagnose you, advise on medication, or monitor emergencies. Human support matters, and you can use MindPal alongside professional care.

The “Help me now” section lists urgent human-support options. MindPal does not contact those services for you. For now, you can choose a practice, read a guide, or finish here.

videos.title: A gentle start to a difficult morning
videos.outline: Make room for a difficult morning. Offer rest, one manageable action or finishing here without a positive-thinking requirement.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
A difficult morning does not need a cheerful beginning. You can take this moment as you are, or finish here.

If it is useful, think only about the next few minutes. Is there something practical you need: a little quiet, rest, or help from someone? There is no requirement to choose an activity.

You might make one task smaller, or leave it for later. What is manageable depends on your circumstances, your energy and your surroundings.

If these words do not fit today, you can leave them aside. MindPal offers choices, not a test of how well you cope. You can seek human support. The ‘Help me now’ section lists urgent-support options.

videos.title: A comfortable pause, with choices
videos.outline: Optional ordinary breathing with no holds or forced pace; external grounding alternative and physical-symptom limits.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
This is an optional pause for everyday stress. You can stop at any time. If breathing exercises are uncomfortable for you, you can try noticing one neutral detail around you instead. You do not need to follow your breath.

If you would like to try, stay in a comfortable position. Let your breath remain at its ordinary depth and pace. No big breath, counting or holding is needed. Notice one breath coming and going, if that feels okay.

If focusing on your breathing brings dizziness, a sense of not getting enough air, discomfort or more panic, stop the exercise. You can shift attention to a neutral detail nearby using a sense that feels comfortable, or finish altogether.

You can stay with that detail briefly, or finish now. There is no need to make a feeling disappear. Seek medical advice for new, persistent or concerning physical symptoms. For severe difficulty breathing or another medical emergency in Australia, call triple zero. This exercise cannot tell you what is causing a symptom.

When you are ready, choose what is manageable next: rest, a small practical action, or support from a person. It is also okay to do nothing further here. You can return to the text guide whenever you want.

videos.title: Notice one steady detail
videos.outline: Notice one neutral external detail; choose any comfortable sense, stop or seek human support.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
You can stop this practice at any time. If it feels okay, notice one ordinary detail near you. Your eyes can stay open.

It might be a colour, the edge of an object, a quiet sound, or a surface supporting you. Choose a sense that feels comfortable enough. There is no correct thing to notice.

Describe one feature to yourself, such as a straight edge or a soft surface. You can pause the video and take your own time.

If this attention feels uncomfortable, stop. You can look elsewhere, change position if comfortable, or choose support from a person.

There is no need to make your feelings disappear. You can finish, rest, or choose one manageable next step. You do not have to decide yet.

videos.title: Grounding without following your breath
videos.outline: External grounding for people who prefer not to focus on breathing; no guaranteed calming outcome.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
You do not need to follow your breathing to take a moment. This is an optional way to notice something outside yourself.

Choose one neutral detail nearby, perhaps a shape, a colour or a quiet sound. Use whichever sense is comfortable for you, or skip this activity.

Notice one feature. You can pause the video for as long or as little as you want.

If noticing this way makes things harder, stop and choose something else. The aim is to offer a choice, not to guarantee a particular feeling. Rest or human support may be more useful. You can finish here.

videos.title: Finding a word for a feeling
videos.outline: Optional feeling words, including mixed and not sure, with a practical-needs alternative.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
A feeling does not need a perfect name. If you want to, choose a word that seems close enough: worried, sad, frustrated, tired, lonely, mixed, or not sure.

You can use your own word, or choose none. There is no need to explain what happened or tell a difficult story.

Perhaps try, I notice some worry. Or, I am not sure what this is. A word describes an experience; it is not a diagnosis.

You might instead ask what you need next: a quieter space, rest, or a safe person to speak with. Choose only what fits your circumstances.

If words make this harder, leave them aside. You can notice an ordinary object nearby or finish. Nothing needs to be written, saved or sent to AI.

videos.title: Words with less pressure
videos.outline: A believable kind or neutral sentence, without excusing harm or requiring positive feelings.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
You do not have to feel positive about a difficult day. If a harsh sentence about yourself is present, you may leave it alone, or try words with less pressure.

This is difficult. I can take one thing at a time. I may need some support.

Choose a sentence only if it feels believable. If kindness feels uncomfortable, something neutral can be enough: I am here, taking a moment.

You can pause, use different words, or stop. This is not a requirement to change how you feel.

You do not have to excuse harmful behaviour from anyone. If someone is hurting or controlling you, support and safety matter.

Perhaps lowering one demand or asking for help would be useful. You do not need to complete an action to finish here.

videos.title: Anxiety: support without solving everything
videos.outline: Everyday anxiety education and choices for human support; new or severe physical symptoms need medical assessment.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
When you describe feeling anxious, you do not have to solve everything in one sitting. This short guide offers choices for everyday wellbeing; it cannot assess or diagnose what you are experiencing.

You might want a practical next step, a short external attention exercise, a break from this screen, or contact with someone who can support you. Breathing exercises are optional. You do not have to use them.

Physical symptoms can have different causes. MindPal cannot tell whether a symptom is anxiety. New, severe or concerning symptoms need medical help. In immediate danger or a medical emergency in Australia, call triple zero.

If worry or distress is affecting your daily life, you can discuss it with a qualified health professional. You do not need a label before asking for support.

For a conversation, you might prepare one question or mention one thing that has been difficult. You can decide what to share. You do not need to retell a painful event here.

You can finish now. You can open ‘Help me now’ for urgent-support options without completing a practice. MindPal does not monitor emergencies or summon help for you.

videos.title: One manageable action
videos.outline: Choose one manageable action, preparation, rest or help; never push through symptoms.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
Think about the next few minutes, rather than the whole day. Is there one small action that might be useful or meaningful? You can also choose rest.

Perhaps place one item where you need it, choose some music, or prepare a question for a person who supports you. Choose something that fits your situation.

You can make the action smaller, prepare without doing it, or decide against it. There is no score for finishing.

If pain, fatigue or your surroundings make it unsuitable, change the action or stop. You do not have to push through symptoms. New or severe symptoms may need medical assessment.

If you try something, you can ask whether it was manageable. The answer can be no. That information may help you choose differently, without judging yourself. You can finish here.

videos.title: One-sentence daily reflection
videos.outline: Optional brief diary reflection, stop if writing adds distress, and explicit local-storage and AI boundaries.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
A reflection can be one sentence, one word, or nothing today. You do not need to explain everything that happened. You can keep this simple and finish whenever you want.

You might choose one question: What felt manageable? What was difficult? Or, what might I need next? Choose only one if it helps. You can also write something entirely different.

If writing makes you feel more stuck or distressed, stop. You could notice something around you, take a break, or reach out for human support. You do not have to turn this into a lesson.

You can reflect without typing anything into MindPal. Before saving personal information, check the privacy information for this version, including where entries are stored and who could access them. On a shared device or browser, someone else may be able to see saved entries. Before using any AI reflection feature, check what text would be sent and how it would be used. You can choose not to use it.

videos.title: Menstrual mood changes: preparing for a care discussion
videos.outline: Specialist review required: optional observations and questions for a clinician; no PMS/PMDD diagnosis or cycle prediction.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
If you have noticed mood changes that seem related to your menstrual cycle, you can bring those observations to a qualified health professional. You do not have to work out a diagnosis yourself.

This guide does not decide whether you have PMS, PMDD, or another condition. MindPal does not predict your cycle or recommend medicines or hormonal treatment.

If keeping notes feels useful, you might record a date, what you noticed, and whether it affected something in daily life. You can keep the note brief. You do not have to record bleeding, intimate details or any information you would rather keep out of an app.

Brief notes may help start a conversation, but they are not a diagnostic assessment. A clinician may suggest daily symptom recording across at least two menstrual cycles to understand a pattern. You do not need to wait or finish a diary before asking for help, especially if symptoms are severe or disrupting daily life.

You can also prepare a question without keeping a diary: I have noticed changes in my mood and would like help understanding them. Or, what information would be useful for our next appointment?

Your experience does not have to fit a regular cycle to deserve attention. You can mention uncertainty, irregular periods, or other changes to the clinician. MindPal will not interpret those details for you.

If recording makes you more distressed or preoccupied, stop. You can ask for support without collecting more information first.

This is an optional pathway. You decide what to save and share with a clinician. If you think you may act on thoughts of suicide or self-harm, or you are in immediate danger, call triple zero in Australia. For crisis support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. You can also find support options in “Help me now”. MindPal does not monitor you or contact help for you.

videos.title: Perimenopause, menopause, mood and asking for support
videos.outline: Specialist review required: questions about mood, sleep and changes for a clinician; no menopause diagnosis or treatment advice.
videos.placeholderLabel: Media placeholder — no HeyGen video generated
videos.transcriptText:
If you have questions about perimenopause—the transition leading up to menopause—menopause itself, or changes in mood or sleep, you can discuss them with a qualified health professional. You do not have to decide on the cause before asking for help.

MindPal cannot diagnose menopause or explain the cause of a mood, sleep or physical symptom. It does not recommend hormonal treatment, supplements or changes to medication.

You might prepare one or two questions for an appointment. For example: I have noticed a change in how I am feeling. What could we consider? Or, what support is available for what is affecting my day?

If notes are useful, keep them in a form that suits you. You could mention when a change started and what you would like help with. You do not have to complete a checklist or share intimate details with an app.

Several things may contribute to changes in mood or sleep. If low mood, anxiety or sleep problems persist or affect daily life, arrange a healthcare appointment rather than assuming they are part of menopause. New, severe or concerning physical symptoms also need medical assessment.

You can choose practical support for today, such as asking someone for help or making one demand smaller. That does not replace healthcare when you need it.

This pathway is optional, and you can leave it at any time. If writing or watching is unhelpful, stop. If you are in immediate danger or think you may act on thoughts of suicide or self-harm, call triple zero in Australia. For crisis support, call Lifeline on 13 11 14. “Help me now” lists further support options.
